subject: Problems with LDSC of user-specified model results

messages.author: 5a635ec53acc6eda
messages.subject: Problems with LDSC of user-specified model results
parts:
Hello all,

I’m running the summary statistics from a GWAS of a user-specified model back through the LDSC function, both to obtain intercepts as a sanity check and to look at genetic covariance with some other relevant phenotypes. In doing so, I've run into two problems. First, I’m losing most of my SNPs, going down to just over 200,000. But these are the same LD-Score files I used when making the LDSC for the user-specified GWAS, so why would it be removing SNPs which would have had to have been in the LD-Score files the first time around?

Second, my intercept is also doing strange things, although perhaps this is related to the above, I’m not sure. I’m getting values very significantly different from 1, both above (~1.4) and below (~0.7). Higher than one I understand to represent confounding due to population stratification, but given that the original sumstats had sensible intercepts, does it make sense that GenomicSEM could introduce stratification like that? It’s conspicuous that the two factors which have this problem are the ones with terms I know to have sample overlap, but I thought GenomicSEM was robust to sample overlap? And significantly lower than one, I’m not sure how to interpret that result. Besides, these are such a radical deviation from what I’m expecting, I’m not sure that they mean anything beyond ‘your GWAS is bad.’ Any ideas as to what might be causing these results?

Thank you,

Lucas

messages.author: 5a635ec53acc6eda
messages.subject: Re: Problems with LDSC of user-specified model results
parts:
Trying to bump this, because I’d still like help on this issue. I’ve tried reverting back to a simpler model, which produces much more sensible intercepts. But seeing as said model is a worse fit without SNP effects, it’d be helpful to know what went wrong with the more complicated model and if it could be addressed. I’ve also tried a model that drops a couple of lower-powered terms, which also produces similarly inflated intercepts. I don’t know if it’s relevant, but both of the models with problematic intercepts are bifactor models, while the model without this issue is a correlated factors model.

Thank you,

Lucas

messages.author: 5a635ec53acc6eda
messages.subject: Re: Problems with LDSC of user-specified model results
parts:
Hi Michel,

I’m not sure I’m understanding your first question. “Factor1”, ect. are the results of a GWAS of a user specified GWAS run in genomicSEM, the summary statistics of which I’m now running back through LDSC. Apologies if I wasn’t clear about that in my initial post. The traits that went into to model I ran were from standard GWAS though.

There are two reasons for the low number of SNPs. The output of the sumstats function was only ~1.6 million SNPs, so that’s all that made it to the GWAS I performed. And from those results, I’ve also done some trimming, both of SNPs that produced lavaan warnings and of SNPs where Z_smooth was over 1.96. Do advise if that’s something I shouldn’t be doing, I’m sure you know more than I do, but that isn’t sufficient to explain the problem. I followed the same trimming procedure on my correlated factors model and produced sensible intercepts. I also just tried running the sumstats from the bifactor model through without pruning, and it produces similar problematic intercepts.

To try to provide more information, I’ve attached two LDSC outputs for my simplified bifactor model, which drops two lower powered terms and consequentially loses factors 2 and 3. These were both run with the same model, but differ in whether I used LDSC or HDL for the covariance matrix. For the one run with LDSC, the intercepts are much the same, despite there being more SNPs. The problem is attenuated somewhat if HDL is used instead of LDSC for the covariance matrix, but not completely. I also distrust the HDL results for unrelated reasons (I get like 3000 significant SNPs, which is pretty hard to believe).

Thank you for your help,

Lucas

messages.subject: Re: Problems with LDSC of user-specified model results
parts:
I get the intercept as a quality control check, hence my concern. I’m pretty surprised to hear you say running a factor GWAS results through LDSC would be likely to cause problems though. The wiki specifically mentions loading results into LDSC as a reason to calculate neff, so why say that if it’s incorrect to do so?

My model (simplified version) looks like so:

model <- ‘Factor1 =~ NA*T1 + T2 + T3 + T4

CommonFactor =~ NA*T1 + T2 + T3 + T4 + T5 + T6 + T7

CommonFactor ~~ 0* Factor1

Factor1 ~ SNP

CommonFactor ~ SNP

T3 ~~ a*T3

a > .001’

Thank you,

Lucas

I’m running the summary statistics from a GWAS of a user-specified model back through the LDSC function, both to obtain intercepts as a sanity check and to look at genetic covariance with some other relevant phenotypes. In doing so, I've run into two problems. First, I’m losing most of my SNPs, going down to just over 200,000. But these are the same LD-Score files I used when making the LDSC for the user-specified GWAS, so why would it be removing SNPs which would have had to have been in the LD-Score files the first time around?

Second, my intercept is also doing strange things, although perhaps this is related to the above, I’m not sure. I’m getting values very significantly different from 1, both above (~1.4) and below (~0.7). Higher than one I understand to represent confounding due to population stratification, but given that the original sumstats had sensible intercepts, does it make sense that GenomicSEM could introduce stratification like that? It’s conspicuous that the two factors which have this problem are the ones with terms I know to have sample overlap, but I thought GenomicSEM was robust to sample overlap? And significantly lower than one, I’m not sure how to interpret that result. Besides, these are such a radical deviation from what I’m expecting, I’m not sure that they mean anything beyond ‘your GWAS is bad.’ Any ideas as to what might be causing these results?

Thank you,

Lucas

Op vr 20 okt. 2023 om 12:03 schreef Lucas Perry <lucascha...@gmail.com>

I get the intercept as a quality control check, hence my concern. I’m pretty surprised to hear you say running a factor GWAS results through LDSC would be likely to cause problems though. The wiki specifically mentions loading results into LDSC as a reason to calculate neff, so why say that if it’s incorrect to do so?

My model (simplified version) looks like so:

model <- ‘Factor1 =~ NA*T1 + T2 + T3 + T4

CommonFactor =~ NA*T1 + T2 + T3 + T4 + T5 + T6 + T7

CommonFactor ~~ 0* Factor1

Factor1 ~ SNP

CommonFactor ~ SNP

T3 ~~ a*T3

a > .001’

Thank you,

Lucas



On Thursday, October 19, 2023 at 8:12:23 PM UTC+1 m.g.n...@gmail.com wrote:
Okay,


this is beginning to make sense now. So why didn't you fit whatever you wanted to fit in one go? why the factor GWAS and then run things trough LDSC? This is fairly likely to cause all kinds of problems. What would you get from LDSC you can't just read out, or fit, in the first model?

Anyway if these intercepts are weird, whatever goes wrong must go wrong at the first stage so we'd need to review your first stage models.


Best,
Michel



On Thu, Oct 19, 2023 at 6:50 PM Lucas Perry <lucascha...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Michel,

I’m not sure I’m understanding your first question. “Factor1”, ect. are the results of a GWAS of a user specified GWAS run in genomicSEM, the summary statistics of which I’m now running back through LDSC. Apologies if I wasn’t clear about that in my initial post. The traits that went into to model I ran were from standard GWAS though.

There are two reasons for the low number of SNPs. The output of the sumstats function was only ~1.6 million SNPs, so that’s all that made it to the GWAS I performed. And from those results, I’ve also done some trimming, both of SNPs that produced lavaan warnings and of SNPs where Z_smooth was over 1.96. Do advise if that’s something I shouldn’t be doing, I’m sure you know more than I do, but that isn’t sufficient to explain the problem. I followed the same trimming procedure on my correlated factors model and produced sensible intercepts. I also just tried running the sumstats from the bifactor model through without pruning, and it produces similar problematic intercepts.

To try to provide more information, I’ve attached two LDSC outputs for my simplified bifactor model, which drops two lower powered terms and consequentially loses factors 2 and 3. These were both run with the same model, but differ in whether I used LDSC or HDL for the covariance matrix. For the one run with LDSC, the intercepts are much the same, despite there being more SNPs. The problem is attenuated somewhat if HDL is used instead of LDSC for the covariance matrix, but not completely. I also distrust the HDL results for unrelated reasons (I get like 3000 significant SNPs, which is pretty hard to believe).

Thank you for your help,

Lucas

bw
